items.name: STOP technique card
items.body: For the moment anger starts building. The gap already exists — this makes it longer.

steps.title: Stop
steps.text: Pause before you do or say anything.

steps.title: Take a breath
steps.text: One slow breath in, one slow breath out.

steps.title: Observe
steps.text: What am I feeling, and how strong is it?

steps.title: Proceed
steps.text: Choose what to do next, rather than react.

items.source: A pause-and-notice sequence from cognitive behavioural practice, commonly taught as STOP or STOPP.

items.name: Passive / aggressive / assertive cards
items.body: Same situation, three different responses. Which gets the best result?

cards.title: Says nothing
cards.text: “It's fine, I guess...”

cards.title: Hits back
cards.text: “This is stupid, I'm not doing it!”

cards.title: Names it calmly
cards.text: “I'm finding this frustrating, can I have a minute?”

cards.title: Walks away upset
cards.text: Says nothing and leaves it inside.

cards.title: Shuts it down
cards.text: “Just leave me alone!”

cards.title: Asks for time
cards.text: “I need a minute to calm down, can we talk after?”

items.name: Assertive phrase bank

cards.title: “I'm finding this really frustrating.”

cards.title: “Can I have a minute before we carry on?”
cards.text: Asks for the gap out loud.

cards.title: “I don't agree, but I'm willing to talk about it.”
cards.text: Holds your position without a fight.

cards.title: “I need some space, I'll come back to this.”
cards.text: Leaving on purpose, not storming off.

items.name: How staff can help me
aliases: Copy for class teacher or pastoral file
items.body: Tick the ones that would actually help. Based on what the Department for Education, the EEF and Ofsted say works: knowing the pupil, heading off known triggers, and keeping the same expectations with the support to meet them.

items: Say hello to me at the door, even on a bad day
Notice when I get it right, not only when I get it wrong
Warn me before something changes, so it isn't a surprise
Tell me off quietly, not in front of the class
Ask me what's going on before deciding what happened
Let me use my signal instead of having to explain in the moment
Let me take a short break in the place we agreed
Give me a few seconds to answer before asking again
Give me instructions one at a time
Keep the same rules for me as everyone else, and help me meet them
Let me put it right afterwards instead of just being punished

items.name: Nicotine cycle diagram
items.body: Why cutting down is hard, and why it isn't about willpower.

steps.title: Craving builds
steps.text: The brain signals that it wants nicotine.

steps.title: Use
steps.text: Vaping delivers a fast hit.

steps.title: Short boost
steps.text: A brief feel-good effect.

steps.title: Dip
steps.text: The feeling fades, often below where it started.

steps.title: Craving builds again
steps.text: The dip is what drives the next one. That's chemistry, not weakness.

items.source: The nicotine dependence cycle described in NHS smoking-cessation guidance. Simplified for a school audience.

items.name: Block, report, save evidence step card
items.body: Order matters here — blocking first can hide the evidence.

steps.title: Screenshot first
steps.text: Before anything else. Blocking can hide the original message.

steps.title: Block
steps.text: Stop it reaching you while you decide what to do.

steps.title: Report on the platform
steps.text: Every app has a route. Find it together now, not later.

steps.title: Tell a trusted adult
steps.text: Earlier means more options, not fewer.

cards.note: Good when you're not ready for detail

cards.title: “Can I show you something?”
cards.text: Lets the screen do the explaining.
cards.note: Easiest if you have a screenshot

cards.title: “This happened and I'm not sure what to do.”
cards.text: Asks for help without asking for action.

cards.title: “I need to tell you something.”
cards.text: Direct. Buys you their full attention.

items.name: Catastrophic thinking examples card
items.body: Read each thought, then the fairer version. Aim for balanced, not positive.

cards.title: “If I fail this, everything's ruined.”
cards.text: Fairer: one result rarely decides everything. There are routes past a bad grade.

cards.title: “It has to be perfect or it's pointless.”
cards.text: Fairer: good enough is still good. Perfect isn't on the mark scheme.

cards.title: “Everyone finds this easier than me.”
cards.text: Fairer: most people feel this privately and say nothing.

items.name: Weekly routine template

items.name: Revision session length guide
items.body: A routine you'll actually keep beats a better one you won't.

steps.title: 20 to 30 minutes
steps.text: Focused revision on one thing. Phone in another room.

steps.title: Short break
steps.text: Five minutes, and actually leave the desk.

steps.title: Repeat, then stop
steps.text: Two or three rounds is a good session. More isn't better.

steps.title: Rest is in the plan
steps.text: Not a reward for finishing. Build it in from the start.

items.name: Exam-day coping strategy cards
items.body: Pick two before the day, not on it.

cards.title: Slow breathing
cards.text: In for four, out for six. Five times.

cards.title: Ground yourself
cards.text: Name five things you can see in the hall.

cards.title: A short phrase
cards.text: One line you've chosen in advance.
cards.note: Write it on the front of your pencil case

cards.title: Start anywhere
cards.text: Answer any question you can. Momentum returns.
cards.note: Don't sit staring at question one

items.name: Breathing technique guide
items.body: Practise this now, in the room. It has to be familiar before it's needed.

steps.title: In for four
steps.text: Through the nose, slowly.

steps.title: Hold for two
steps.text: No need to strain.

steps.title: Out for six
steps.text: Through the mouth. Longer out than in is the whole trick.

steps.title: Four or five times
steps.text: Any more and you'll feel light-headed.

items.source: Paced breathing with a longer out-breath, in common clinical and pastoral use.

items.name: Aggression cycle diagram
items.body: Five phases, not four. The old version stopped at the action — but what happens after is where most of the harm gets repaired or repeated.

steps.title: Trigger
steps.text: Something happens. It can be instant, or slow-burning like tiredness or being nagged.

steps.title: Escalation
steps.text: Fists clench, breathing goes shallow, you start pacing. This is where it can still be stopped.

steps.title: Crisis
steps.text: The moment it becomes physical. Thinking has gone offline.

steps.title: Recovery
steps.text: Coming down. It takes far longer than it took to go up, and it's easy to set off again.

steps.title: After
steps.text: Tired, flat, often ashamed. This is when putting it right is possible.

items.note: Escalation is the phase where anything you do still works
items.source: The aggression cycle (Reilly et al., 1994; Videbeck, 2014), the five-phase model widely used in UK school behaviour training.

items.name: Avoidance ladder template
items.body: Six things you'd get out of if you could, the easiest at the top. Look at the examples, then fill in your own. A first step is always smaller than the thing itself.
items.source: Graded exposure, as described in DfE statutory guidance Working together to improve school attendance and in cognitive behavioural practice.

cards.title: Walking into maths late
cards.text: First step: wait outside the door for the last few minutes of break, so you walk in with everyone else.

cards.title: The lunch hall
cards.text: First step: go in with one person, stay two minutes, then leave.

cards.title: Answering in class
cards.text: First step: answer one question you already know the answer to.
cards.note: Pick the easy one on purpose

items.name: Grounding technique card
items.body: Techniques for an anxious moment.

cards.title: Slow breathing: 4 in, 6 out
cards.text: In through your nose for 4 seconds, out through your mouth for 6.

cards.title: 5-4-3-2-1 senses
cards.text: Name 5 things you see, 4 you hear, 3 you feel.

cards.title: Hold something with texture
cards.text: Hold an object and describe how it feels to yourself.

cards.title: Name where you are
cards.text: Say the room, the day and the time, out loud or in your head.

items.source: Sensory grounding, including the 5-4-3-2-1 method, in common clinical and pastoral use.

items.name: Disengagement trigger cards
items.body: Sort into most-relevant-to-me order.

cards.title: Task feels too hard
cards.text: You can't see a way into it.

cards.title: Task feels too easy
cards.text: There's nothing in it to hold you.

cards.title: Room is too noisy
cards.text: Too much sound to think through.

cards.title: I feel tired
cards.text: Not enough sleep, or a long day already.

cards.title: Distracted by a friend
cards.text: Someone nearby keeps pulling your attention.

cards.title: Don't understand the instructions
cards.text: You missed the start and didn't ask.

cards.title: I feel bored
cards.text: Time is dragging and nothing holds you.

cards.title: I feel hungry
cards.text: Your body needs something before your brain works.

items.name: Trusted-adult discussion prompts
items.body: Openers for a conversation, not a checklist to work through.

cards.title: Who do you trust?
cards.text: An adult in or out of school.

cards.title: What's different about them?
cards.text: What do they do that others don't?

cards.title: What would make you more likely to listen?
cards.text: One thing an adult could do differently.

items.body: Explore a recent incident with a specific staff member.

rows: What the adult might have been managing

aliases: Perspective-taking worksheet, adapted for staff relationships

items.name: Respectful disagreement script card
items.body: Three parts: tone, timing, wording. Timing is the one that gets missed.

cards.title: “Can I talk to you about this after the lesson?”
cards.text: Not in front of the class, not in the first ten seconds.
cards.note: This one does most of the work

cards.title: “I don't think that's fair — can you explain why?”
cards.text: Asks rather than accuses.

cards.title: “I hear you, but can we find another way?”
cards.text: Acknowledges them first.

items.name: Restorative conversation prompt card
items.body: For repairing one working relationship the pupil still needs.

cards.title: What happened?
cards.text: Both sides get asked this.

cards.title: What were you thinking at the time?
cards.text: Not an excuse — context.

cards.title: Who has been affected, and how?
cards.text: Including the wider class.

cards.title: What would help this relationship going forward?
cards.text: Something specific and small.

items.name: Working relationship plan template
items.body: Agreed with one or two key staff.

items.name: Low-pressure activity ideas
items.body: For week one. Let the pupil pick, and work side by side rather than face to face.

cards.title: Drawing or colouring
cards.text: No pressure to talk at all.

cards.title: A shared game
cards.text: Cards, a puzzle, a quiz.

cards.title: Their own interests
cards.text: Games, shows, music, sport.

cards.title: A shared task
cards.text: Tidying or organising something together.

items.name: Barriers-to-connecting card sort
items.body: Sort into most-relevant-to-me order.

cards.title: Feeling different
cards.text: Like you don't fit the group you're in.

cards.title: Past rejection or bullying
cards.text: It went badly before, so why try again.

cards.title: Not knowing how to join in
cards.text: You want to, but not how to start.

cards.title: Loud or busy spaces
cards.text: Crowds make it harder to think or speak.

cards.title: Worried about saying the wrong thing
cards.text: You replay it before you've said it.

cards.title: Preferring to be alone sometimes
cards.text: Not every quiet moment is a problem.

cards.title: Low confidence
cards.text: You assume they'd rather you weren't there.

cards.title: Not knowing who to sit with
cards.text: The moment at the door when you have to choose.

items.name: Conversation starter cards
items.body: Simple openers to try.

cards.title: “Can I sit here?”
cards.text: Short, direct, and easy to say yes to.

cards.title: “What are you playing?”
cards.text: Asks about them, not about you.

cards.title: “That looks fun, can I join?”
cards.text: Names what you noticed, then asks.

cards.title: “What did you think of that?”
cards.text: Works after any shared lesson or event.

cards.title: “Have you played this before?”
cards.text: Gives them something easy to answer.

cards.title: “Mind if I watch for a bit?”
cards.text: A way in without having to join straight away.
